title: Timothy
lead: Timothy was Paul's closest coworker: a young man from Lystra with a Jewish mother and a Greek father, who joined Paul on his second journey, carried his messages to the churches, and is named as co-sender of six of Paul's letters. Two letters of the New Testament are addressed to him.

sections.b: Acts meets him at Lystra in Asia Minor: "a disciple was living there, Timothy by name. His mother was a Jewish believer, and his father a Greek" (Acts 16:1). Paul "took Timothy and circumcised him, on account of the Jews living in that area, since everyone knew his father was Greek" (Acts 16:3). Whether the son of a Jewish mother counted as a Jew then is debated (Shaye Cohen's study is a classic treatment); see the notes on Acts 16. 2 Timothy 1:5 names his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and 2 Timothy 3:15 says he knew the holy writings from childhood.

Timothy traveled with Paul through Macedonia and Greece (Acts 17:14-15; Acts 18:5), was sent ahead into Macedonia from Ephesus (Acts 19:22), and was in the party traveling with Paul toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). Paul sent him to Thessalonica to strengthen the new church (1 Thessalonians 3:2, 6), to Corinth as "my beloved and faithful child in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 4:17; 1 Corinthians 16:10), and planned to send him to Philippi (Philippians 2:19-22). He is co-sender of 2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians and Philemon, and he greets the Romans (Romans 16:21). Hebrews 13:23 mentions that "our brother Timothy" has been released.

sections.b:
1 Timothy pictures him left in Ephesus to stop certain people from teaching other doctrines (1 Timothy 1:3), young enough that some might look down on him (1 Timothy 4:12), set apart by prophecy and the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 1:18; 4:14), and often unwell (1 Timothy 5:23). 2 Timothy calls him to come to Paul in prison before winter (2 Timothy 4:9, 21). Readers who think the letters are later than Paul take this Timothy partly as a model for church leaders of the writer's own day; readers who hold Paul's authorship take him as the real man in a real situation.

Eusebius (Church History 3.4) records the tradition that Timothy was the first to hold the office of overseer (bishop) in Ephesus, as Titus was in Crete.
